notes.meaning: David ruled a small kingdom, yet he says the whole earth belongs to the LORD. That includes everything in it and every person who lives on it, even people who do not know God. People may claim land and kingdoms, but God is the true owner, and what we have is only lent to us. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 10:26 to show that food offered to idols does not really belong to idols.

Here is the reason the world is God's: he made it. The picture comes from Genesis 1:9, where God makes dry land rise out of the waters. He also keeps it standing, so the seas cannot swallow it. A world resting on water also reminds us that earthly things are not a safe place to build our hopes.

The "hill of the LORD" is Mount Zion, where God's holy tent and the ark were. The ark was the sacred chest that showed God was present. To "stand" there means to serve before God and be welcomed by him. The question asks who is fit to come near a holy God. The earthly hill also points beyond itself to God's people and to heaven.

Hands stand for what we do, and the heart stands for what we think and want. So God looks for a good life on the outside and a sincere heart on the inside. Not lifting up the soul to an idol means not setting your heart on empty things like money, praise or pleasure, or on false gods. Not swearing deceitfully means being honest and keeping your promises. Christians see that only Jesus fully meets this standard, and we come to God through him.

This person receives blessing and "vindication," which the older versions call "righteousness." It means being right with God, and it comes as a gift. These people are not earning their way up the hill. As Matthew Henry puts it, "we have no righteousness of our own." God gives them good things, makes them holy, and in the end saves them. Adam Clarke thinks there may be a hint here of Obed-edom, whose house God blessed while the ark stayed there.

People like this are God's true family. They are the real "Jacob," or Israel, marked out not by birth but by seeking God. To seek God's "face" means to seek his favour and friendship. "Selah" is a musical word; Adam Clarke takes it as meaning "It is true." Some old copies and translations read "O God of Jacob," as the BSB does here. Others read simply "O Jacob," meaning God's people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 7-10 were first a separate victory song that was later joined to verses 1-6. Others answer that the two parts belong together, both centred on God coming to Zion.

notes.meaning: Many think David wrote this for the day the ark was carried up to Zion. The marchers reach the gates and call out to them as if the gates were people. The gates are told to lift their heads, as if even they were too small for so great a King. Christians also hear in this verse two more things. One is Jesus rising into heaven and heaven's gates opening for him and for us. The other is Jesus asking to come into our hearts (Revelation 3:20).

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: An old reading, still used in the Orthodox church, takes the gates in verses 7-10 as the gates of the place of the dead. Christ breaks in after his death to free the faithful who died before him. Gill reports a Catholic form of this view.

notes.meaning: The gatekeepers ask, "Who is this King of Glory?" The answer comes back loud and strong: the LORD, the mighty warrior. This echoes Exodus 15:3, where God is praised for winning Israel's battles. Christians also see here Christ's victory over sin, death and Satan.

The call to the gates is repeated, the way songs often repeat a line. The repetition stresses how important this is. It also wakes up dull hearts that are slow to make room for God. Adam Clarke pictures the gatekeepers holding back at first, so that the King can be described even more fully.

The question comes again, more eager this time, and the final answer is the high point of the psalm: the LORD of Hosts. "Hosts" means armies. God commands all the powers of heaven and earth, including angels, stars and every creature. With that, the gates open and God enters Zion. Christians rejoice that Jesus, the risen and ascended Saviour, is this King of Glory.
